zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical coverage was checked after independent scan reading against Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . The scan-derived transcription and English review notes are this review’s work; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

runs.text: Aßi, ou não ſei como. Vt,

lines.note: Toyakakuya expresses uncertainty about this or that way; the Portuguese says “thus, or I do not know how.” The initial is T, not OCR r, and the negative is não, not mão.

Toyakakuya to yuu uchi ni begins an example about talking over this and that. The damaged speaking form is read yǔ: the scan shows a caron over its abraded u, rather than the OCR yui. The Portuguese em quanto continues across the line break.

runs.text: to fallão decà, & delà, ou ſe ſera aßi, ou não,

lines.note: Continues em quanto: while people discuss this or that, whether it will be so or otherwise. The scan supports fallão with f and the completed aßi; decà and delà retain the printed grave marks.
The final alternative, “or in what manner,” completes the preceding example of indecision. This short continuation is independent physical lineation, not a new entry.
Tooyakata is glossed as a prince who is the son of a yakata, a lord. Yacata is a Japanese title embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the scan supports Y rather than OCR V and retains italic type.

runs.text: O não ſaber que ſe faça,

lines.note: Toyasen kakuyasen describes not knowing what one should do, a deliberative this-way-or-that-way expression. The Portuguese translates that uncertainty directly.
The alternative “or what counsel to take” completes the preceding deliberative definition. No independent Japanese wording is supplied on this continuation.

runs.text: Gente, ou ſoldados que ſe acre-

lines.note: Toehatae refers here to increased numbers of people or soldiers. The Portuguese acrescentão is divided after acre- and must remain on its two physical rows.
Completes acrescentão em numero, then begins an example with toehatae ni tori-. The Japanese compound verb continues in the next row.

runs.text: Cercar com muita gente, ou com

lines.note: Mawasu completes torimawasu, surrounding or encircling. The gloss specifies doing so with many people, introducing its second formulation below.
“Many circles of people” completes the encirclement gloss. The close printed spacing in degente is retained rather than silently normalizing it.
Tooyoo denotes a present need; tooyoo ni introduces the example completed by tatsu. The first o has a caron and the second a circumflex in the printed headword and example.

runs.text: Preſtar, ou ſeruir em algũa nece-

lines.note: Tatsu completes tooyoo ni tatsu, to be useful for a current need. The Portuguese necessity noun is split after nece-; its historical letterforms are retained.
Completes necessidade presente, the present need for which something is useful. This is a genuine short continuation.

runs.text: Pao que ſe prèga ao comprido na om

lines.note: Toyose is a wooden piece fixed lengthwise along a door jamb. The printed om ends the row without an inferred hyphen, despite continuing as ombreira below.

runs.text: breira da porta pera q̃ entre a porta, & a ombrei

lines.note: The description places the strip between the door and the jamb. The abbreviated q̃ is retained, and ombreira is again divided without adding an absent terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ra não fique eſpaço aberto pera poder ver, ou me

lines.note: Explains the purpose: leaving no open gap through which one can see or insert something. The final me continues into meter on the next row without a supplied hyphen.
“Put the fingers in” completes the protective function of the door strip. The short row belongs to Toyoxe above.

runs.text: Certo azeite como verniz, ou charão.

lines.note: Tooyuu is a particular oil compared with varnish or lacquer. The circumflex and the historical Portuguese charão are retained; the gloss does not itself establish a botanical species.
Tooza is explained by ataru za, the present seat or place, then as the house where people are gathered. The headword has a caron, unlike the preceding oil entry.

runs.text: eſtà gente. ¶ Item, Adu. Agora de

lines.note: Completes the gathering-place sense, then marks an adverbial use meaning “now.” Adu. is part of the italic explanatory apparatus.
The adverbial gloss means at present or at this juncture. Toozano co- begins the next example and joins to koto across the physical line break.

runs.text: Couſa dagora, ou breue, & q̃ logo paßa.

lines.note: Koto completes the phrase for a present or fleeting affair. The Portuguese adds that it is brief and passes immediately.
Toozai is identified with higashi and nishi, east and west. The Portuguese prints Oeste, not the OCR reading Deste; the spelling and provisional st allograph are otherwise kept.
Toozai nanboku enumerates east, west, south and north; the Portuguese orders the last two as north and south. Oeste is one word in the scan, correcting the OCR initial and internal break.
The Portuguese completes Norte and Sul. Toozai ni chisoo suru means bustling to and fro to provide hospitality; the scan has z in Tôzaini and italic Fa-, not the provisional mixed-type fragment.

runs.text: zer muito agaſalhado mouẽdoſe de cà pera là.

lines.note: Completes fazer and explains the effortful hospitality: moving from here to there. The historical agaſalhado and abbreviation tilde in mouẽdoſe are preserved.

runs.text: Fora, ou couſa de fora que não he de

lines.note: Tozama is outside or an outside thing, leading into a contrast with what is internal or familiar. The Portuguese definition is not yet limited to a formal political status.
Completes the contrast with inside or familiar, then introduces tozama no hito, an outside person. The example is continuous with the alternative below.
Hokasama no hito is offered as an alternative to tozama no hito. The Portuguese means an outsider; the lower-case l is the Latin alternative marker.
“One who is not familiar” completes the outsider gloss. This row is explanatory continuation rather than a distinct noun.

runs.text: Homẽs que ſeruem a algum ſenhor

lines.note: Tozamashuu denotes men serving a lord from elsewhere. The scan supports plural Homẽs without the OCR comma; the following row supplies the condition of distance.
The men are absent or far away while serving their lord. The historical Portuguese absent form is retained as printed.
Too-zan, paraphrased as ataru yama, is this mountain or this temple. The initial T corrects OCR r; the embedded Japanese temple word Tera begins as Te- and continues below.

runs.text: ra que ordinariamente està em monte.

lines.note: Ra completes Tera, and the gloss explains that such a temple is ordinarily on a mountain. The fragment is part of the Japanese term embedded in Portuguese and retains its italic setting.

Toozan, yamani noboru, literally going up the mountain, introduces the practice of boys going to Buddhist temples. The printed Oirem is retained together; it functions as a Portuguese nominal infinitive construction.

runs.text: às Teras dos Bonzos a aprender aler, & eſcre-

lines.note: The boys go to the bonzes’ temples to learn to read and write. The print has Teras, a pluralized Japanese temple term embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation, rather than OCR Peras.

runs.text: uer, & quando os pais os tirão da Tera que or

lines.note: Completes eſcreuer, then describes parents taking the boys out of the temple. Tera is the Japanese term embedded in the italic gloss; or begins ordinariamente on the next physical row without an inferred hyphen.

runs.text: dinariamente he depois de 3. annos, diz ſe,

lines.note: The departure ordinarily occurs after three years; diz ſe introduces what that departure is called. This is the dictionary’s own description of the schooling practice.

Gueſan ſuru, corresponding to leaving or descending from the temple, supplies the contrasted term. The Portuguese says to leave the temple where the boys were learning; printed s is not modernized from the expected lexical identity.

runs.text: aler, & eſcreuer. ¶ Item, Ir à Tera, ou

lines.note: Completes learning to read and write, then adds the wider use “go to a temple.” Tera remains the Japanese noun embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation.
The broader definition includes any other people going to a temple or pagoda. Varela is the Portuguese glossing term here, not a new Japanese headword.
A separate Toozan is paraphrased by higashi yama, an eastern mountain. Both the initial T and Portuguese Oriente are supported by the scan, correcting OCR F and D.
“Toward the east” supplies the alternative orientation of the mountain. It completes the previous entry and must not be absorbed into the next verb.
Tozashi, tozasu, tozaita means closing a door. The historical -aita principal part is preserved; the example begins with To-, the door object.
Uo tozasu completes to wo tozasu, closing the door. The printed line division splits the object phrase across rows without changing its interpretation.
Toozoku is equated with nusubito and glossed as thieves. The faded initial T remains visible and is restored; the caron is kept rather than normalized to a modern spelling.

U is equated with usagi, the hare. The decorated V is the headword’s initial and extends beside six rows; it is not the spurious numeral in the OCR. Its Portuguese description continues with the zodiac count.
The hare is one of the twelve animals or signs. The scan reads 12. animaes, replacing the broken OCR r2 and antmaes; onde is divided across the line ending.

runs.text: de os Iapões contão os annos, &

lines.note: Completes onde and explains that the Japanese count years by these signs. Os annos corrects the OCR’s compressed orannos; the sentence continues to the hours.
The signs also designate hours. U no koku, the hour of the hare, introduces the printed clock-time explanation continued below.

runs.text: cinco horas atè as 6. de polla-

lines.note: The dictionary gives the period from five until six in the morning. The printed numeral is 6, not the OCR’s accented ô; the supplied historical hours are retained without converting them to a modern convention.
Completes polla-menhãa, “in the morning.” The visible tilde is over the first of the two a types in this impression; the supplied menhãa is retained rather than moved to match a general expectation.
A second u is the cormorant, explained by u no tori. Vno begins the proverb below; the punctuation after the explanatory i is a comma in the scan.
The proverb says that a crow imitating a cormorant will swallow water. The print retains mizzu curǒ; the Portuguese rendering explains the resulting drowning.

runs.text: que quer mergulhar como o coruo marinho afo-

lines.note: The crow tries to dive like the cormorant. The Portuguese afogar-se is divided after afo-, with its continuation on the next row.

runs.text: garſe ha: diz ſe dos que intentão couſas ſobre ſu-

lines.note: The crow will drown; the proverb applies to people attempting things beyond their capacity. The visible colon after ha separates the result from the explanation of the proverb.
As completes suas forças, their powers. U no me, taka no me introduces the sharp eyes of a cormorant and a hawk; the Portuguese olhos begins as O-.
Completes olhos and describes lively, keen eyes. U nomi wo su- begins the further expression for swallowing something whole.

runs.text: Engulir algũa couſa ſem mastigar. No

lines.note: Ru completes suru. The gloss specifies swallowing without chewing, then introduces a regional comparison with No on the next row.
Cami identifies the upper-region usage, where the expression is Vnnomini ſuru. The doubled n is retained from the print; Cami is Japanese embedded in Portuguese, not an ordinary entry headword.

runs.text: Auer: mas não ſe vſa ſò por ſi.

lines.note: U is equated with aru, being or existing, and the Portuguese warns that it is not used alone. Vto starts the example combining affirmation and negation below.
Vto mo mutomo fenji nai says there was no reply of either yes or no. Xid. is retained as the printed citation label; the Portuguese reſpõdeo is divided at the row boundary.

runs.text: deo de ſi, ou de não. ¶

lines.note: Completes the reply example. The next phrase, u-mu ni hatasoozu, promises completion regardless; the visible spacing V muni is retained, and the final verb continues below.

runs.text: Em todo caſo, ou por fas, & por ne-

lines.note: Zu completes the resolve to finish the task. The Portuguese paraphrases this as in any case, whether by fair or foul means, dividing nefas across the row break.
Faz completes the printed ne-faz construction, and o eide acabar states “I shall finish it.” The historical written form eide is retained.

runs.text: Particula de que ſe vſa desta maneira.

lines.note: Wa is introduced as a particle and the following rows illustrate its use. The V is a two-row enlarged initial in roman type, not italic OCR punctuation.
Nusumi wa tsukamatsuranu means “as for stealing, I do not do it.” The Portuguese topic construction quanto he begins with Quã- here.

runs.text: to he furtar não o faço. ¶

lines.note: Completes the translation denying theft. Yomi wa yome begins the contrasting example that acknowledges reading while withholding understanding.
Domo completes the concessive yomedo(mo); gatten xenu says that the speaker does not understand. The Portuguese por em is divided between rows and is kept in its printed form.

runs.text: em não entendo. Iunta tambẽ esta particula aos

lines.note: Completes “but I do not understand,” then describes the particle joined to participles. Em is the continuation of por above; tambẽ retains the abbreviation tilde.
The dictionary equates this attached use with naraba or koto wa. These forms occur within the grammatical explanation and are upright; italic Vt, introduces the example below.
Hitobito wo tatazumaxete wa busata ja means that leaving people standing is discourteous. The Portuguese fazer begins as Fa at the edge, with no inferred hyphen.

runs.text: zer eſperar em pè os homẽs à porta he falta.

lines.note: Completes fazer and specifies leaving the people waiting on their feet at the door. The gloss evaluates this as a fault or lack of courtesy.

Wa is glossed by the damaged printed Yau raguru, pointing to yawaraguru, but is said always to be used with shi/suru. The internal a expected in the Japanese synonym is not securely visible, so its provisional spacing is retained. Enlarged comparison with the clear commas later on this row supports Mas: its faint final short s occupies the letter body above the baseline, rather than the below-baseline position of a comma.
Suru completes the conjugational pair after com above. The full construction means explaining or interpreting into another language; the upright verb is embedded in the Portuguese usage statement.

A separate wa denotes a Zen subject for contemplation, explained as Ienxǔno coſocu. The long-u mark and adjoining type are abraded; the supplied caron is retained provisionally rather than replaced from expectation.
The meditation topics are those assigned by Zen practitioners. Ienxùs is the Japanese sect name pluralized within the Portuguese explanation, with the printed grave retained.
Wa here means a wheel or circle. This brief independent entry is distinct from the preceding Zen term.
Waa is an exclamation of astonishment. Interjeição preserves the printed Portuguese spelling and must not be conflated with the preceding wa noun.
Wabi, waburu, wabita covers asking mercy or pleading. The principal parts retain the historical -uru conjugation; the Portuguese rogar is divided after ro-.
Completes rogar, adds becoming sad, then begins the explanation of a compound-verb use with Iũ-to. The printed capital I and tilde replace the OCR tũ fragment.

runs.text: to à raiz de outros verbos, Fazer com difficul-

lines.note: When joined to another verb’s stem, wabi conveys doing the action with difficulty. Verbos and difficul- are supported by the scan, correcting OCR verbot and diffical-.

runs.text: dade o que ſignifica o verbo a que ſe ajunta. Vt,

lines.note: Completes dificuldade and explains that the difficulty applies to the action of the attached verb. Italic Vt, introduces the illustrative compounds.

Hito wo tazune waburu means having difficulty finding someone. The damaged internal a of vaburu is compatible with the supplied reading and the surrounding principal forms; the Portuguese gloss starts “seek someone with”.
Trabalho completes the difficult search. Machiwaburu then illustrates waiting with difficulty or distress, continued in Portuguese below.
The waiting gloss concludes with difficulty or pain. Wabita tei de goza- begins a further example describing a distressed or impoverished appearance.
Ru completes gozaru; the Portuguese describes the signs and manner of a person being poor. Mostras, rather than OCR Mosiras, is the visible noun; the close printed estarpobre spacing is retained.
